title: How Great Teachers Teach Lessons (Their Secrets)
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that lesson delivery, not just behavior management, is what separates great teachers from their peers, since lessons form the backbone of daily classroom work and dominate great teachers' thinking. He presents a list of 24 traits shared by exceptional lesson-givers, including deep content knowledge, single-objective focus, storytelling and playacting over show-and-tell, obsessive checking for understanding, and a near-total shift of responsibility onto students during independent work. He anticipates and directly addresses skeptical reactions ('that may work in the suburbs,' 'my students don't pay attention') by insisting the approach works everywhere, from Portland to the Potomac, and that it is being proven in schools serving all kinds of students. His concrete advice is not to attempt wholesale adoption immediately but to try each practice in small doses, improving incrementally, on the premise that this incremental effort compounds into transformed teaching over time.
points: Great teachers go deep on fewer objectives rather than wide across many, and they eschew most prepackaged guidebooks and resources.
They story-tell, playact, and paint vivid mental pictures instead of relying on show-and-tell to build understanding.
They check for understanding obsessively and accept nothing less than full student success before releasing a lesson to independent work.
The approach isn't reserved for suburban or advantaged schools; Linsin insists it works in any school when actually implemented.
Rather than trying to adopt every trait at once, teachers should try each practice a little at a time and improve daily.
quotes: Great teachers teach lessons differently than their colleagues. It’s why their students are more engaged, productive, studious, and academically competent.
But lessons form the backbone of their everyday work. Lessons are what dominate their thinking because they never forget that educating students is the point.
I want to challenge you by saying that this approach and is being done in schools from Portland to the Potomac. It works everywhere and it changes lives.
It’s to upend your assumptions. It’s to throw a wrench into the lie that students at your school, classroom, or neighborhood can’t listen, learn, and behave.
In the meantime, challenge yourself. Throw away the excuses. Try each bullet point just a little. Get better each day.
